opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it made me a bit reflective, maybe even a little humbled. When you're doing the work, you never think about whether something will last ten years. You're a student, you're worried about the deadline, whether the experiments will finish, whether reviewers will understand the idea. So getting recognized a decade later is a strange feeling. It's like receiving a letter from your younger self.

The biggest lesson for me is that the papers that last usually aren't the ones chasing the leaderboard. A benchmark number gets beaten in six months. What survives is a simple idea that people can carry into contexts you never imagined. At the time, we were asking a fairly basic question about how to make deep networks learn better and more transparently. That simplicity is probably why it stayed useful.

It also changed how I think about my own taste. Today the field moves incredibly fast, and there's a lot of pressure to follow whatever is hot that month. The award reminded me that it's okay, maybe even necessary, to work on things that look a little unfashionable, as long as you believe the question is fundamental. Time is a much better reviewer than any conference committee.

And lastly, it made me think about collaboration and mentorship. None of this was done alone. A lot of what I value now as a professor, giving students room to explore, encouraging them to pursue ideas that are clean rather than merely impressive, comes from that experience. If my students can write something that still matters in ten years, that would mean much more to me than any single award.

r001.rationale: The candidate says recognition a decade later prompted reflection and contrasts short-term research pressures with ideas that endure, explicitly framing time as a better reviewer.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, that award was a strange experience, because it forced me to look back at work I did ten years ago, and the version of me who did it was not thinking about anything like a "test of time." I was a PhD student trying to get a paper accepted. If you had told me then that ResNeXt would still be something people cite and build on a decade later, I would have laughed.

The thing that really changed for me is my sense of what matters in a piece of research. When you are in the middle of it, you obsess over benchmark numbers, over beating the previous state of the art by half a point. But looking back, none of that is why the work survived. What survived was a simple idea, a clean design principle, something people could take and adapt without needing our exact code or our exact setup. The results table from 2017 is irrelevant now. The idea is still useful.

So I have become a lot more skeptical of complexity. A lot of papers today, including some of my own, add more and more components, and each one gives you a little gain. But when I ask myself, "what in this will someone still care about in ten years," usually the honest answer is one small thing, or nothing. That question has become a filter for me. If I can't articulate the one idea in a sentence, I'm probably not done thinking.

The other effect is more personal. It made me more patient. Research culture right now moves very fast, every week there is a new model, a new leaderboard, and it's easy to feel that if you are not shipping something every month you are falling behind. The award was a reminder that impact works on a very different timescale. The things that ended up mattering most were not the things that got the most attention when they came out. So I try to tell my students, and myself, to worry a bit less about the reaction next week and a bit more about whether the work is actually right.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the award made them look back at work from ten years earlier and reminded them that research impact unfolds on a very different timescale.

astra-6.text:
It made me think more about the time horizon of research. When you’re working on a paper, you’re focused on getting the idea to work, running the experiments, and meeting the deadline. It’s much harder to know which parts will still matter years later.

So, for me, the award was an encouragement to be patient and to focus on the underlying question. A benchmark result gives you immediate feedback, but whether an idea helps other people think about a problem or build something new takes time to see. That’s the kind of contribution I want to aim for, even though you can’t predict it in advance.

r001.rationale: The candidate says research’s lasting impact takes time to see and describes the award as encouragement to be patient, but it does not connect that realization to the award’s ten-year retrospective evaluation.

sol-6.1.text:
It made me think more about the time horizon of research. When you finish a paper, you’re focused on the immediate results: Does it work? Will people find it useful? But whether an idea lasts is something you can only learn much later, through what other people do with it.

So for me, the award was a reminder to be patient and to care about the underlying question. A benchmark result can get attention today, but I’d like to work on ideas that people can still build on years from now. You can’t predict which ideas will have that kind of impact, but you can let that longer perspective guide the problems you choose.

r001.rationale: The response discusses research lasting over time and adopting a longer perspective, but does not connect this realization to the award’s ten-year retrospective evaluation.
